Why Docker for MySQL?

Real persistence means a real database server running somewhere — Docker is the fastest way to get one.

Everything so far has run against an in-memory array — no separate process to install, configure, or even think about. A real database is different: MySQL is a server process of its own, with its own installation, its own configuration, its own running instance to manage, entirely independent of Node or this project.

You already know MySQL itself from Laravel — the SQL, the relational model, none of that is new. What's new is running it locally without a framework like Laravel/Herd/XAMPP setting it up for you behind the scenes. Docker solves that by packaging MySQL (server, default config, the lot) into a container image you can start and stop as a single unit, with nothing installed on your machine except Docker itself.

Docker Compose goes one step further: instead of typing a long docker run command with every option spelled out, you describe the containers your project needs in one YAML file, and docker compose up starts them all. This project's docker-compose.yml will hold exactly one service for now — mysql — with redis and the API itself joining later in Week 6; the app itself keeps running directly on your machine with npm run dev throughout, for a fast edit-reload loop that a container would only slow down.
